utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed, Mr. Lukic, that Mr. Mladic has expressed that he, for medical reasons, is unable to attend. We have, however, not seen yet any medical confirmation of this -- these medical reasons. Could you inform the Chamber, could you tell us what you know and where we are at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know -- I don't know much more than Your Honours, since I was informed by the guard this morning that Mr. Mladic was not here when I asked to visit him. And my co-counsel called me later on to tell me that Mr. Mladic informed him that he doesn't feel well, and our intention is to go and visit him as soon as possible to check and see if it's possible at least to have a trial tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether we have a trial tomorrow, whether we have a trial today, depends on the medical situation, I would say. The Chamber has asked the Registry to provide a medical report on shortest notice. We will then -- well, see what it says. If there's any confirmed medical reason, of course, we'll wait until Mr. Mladic is well enough to attend court. If the medical report says that there's no medical reason not for him to attend, then we most likely would proceed. And, of course, if you have any additional information on the basis of any of the counsel visiting Mr. Mladic, we would like to hear that. I also understand, just for completeness, that Mr. Mladic did not sign any waiver form. So we'll not proceed until then. We would have quite a number of very practical matters, such as replacement of translations, or putting on the record some decisions which the Defence is aware of already. We would not even deal with those, unless you say, Well, these purely practical matters, we can proceed with those. Then, of course, we would proceed, but not without the consent of the Defence, the Defence being the accused and/or counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you want -- if you say, No, I'd rather wait until Mr. Mladic has had an opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I would rather wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even for putting on the record replacement of translations, et cetera, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course not. For those technical issues, we can sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I -- under those circumstances, if you say that we can proceed with that, then we would do that. I have quite a list after the couple of weeks since we have not been in court. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will not read any of the decisions which even in cases where the -- where the Defence is already aware of the outcome of that decision, but we'll wait for either Mr. Mladic to be present or for a medical report before we deal with that. At the same time, decisions already known to the Defence to put them on the record, Mr. Mladic -- Mr. Lukic, I take it that that should be no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any observations from the Defence -- from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to proceed with a few matters. First, the Chamber has decided at the request of the Defence not to sit on Monday, the 6th of May, 2013, and that decision is hereby put on the record. Then next item. The Chamber hereby puts on the record its confidential decision which was issued on the 13th of March, 2013, denying a request by the accused to amend the trial sitting schedule on the basis of health concerns having found that there is no basis for such an amendment and declaring moot a request for permission of verbal communication with the Defence team during the proceedings. Mr. Lukic, when I deal with anything you think would be inappropriate to deal with, then please jump up and tell us. I then move on to the next item. The Chamber was informed by the Registry that Rule 65 ter number 8746 and 8542 were each admitted twice. First, on the 27th of February, 2013, and then on the 1st of March, 2013, respectively. The Registry is instructed to vacate the exhibit numbers assigned to these Rule 65 ter numbers on the 1st of March, 2013. So that was on the second round; namely, D266 and D267. Rule 65 ter 8746 shall remain on the record as D249, and Rule 65 ter 8542 shall remain on the record as D250. I move on to the next item. On the 28th of February of this year, the Chamber reserved exhibit numbers D251 up to and including D260 for possible assignment to documents tendered through Witness RM513 pending discussion on admission of these documents, discussion between the parties. On the 1st of March, the Defence clarified that it sought admission of only four of these documents - that is, D255, D257, D259, and D260 - which were admitted into evidence under seal. The Chamber hereby puts on the record that the six remaining reserved exhibit numbers are therefore vacated. I move on to the next one, which is about the military lexicon. On the 1st of March, 2013, the -- at the Chamber's instruction, the Registry assigned exhibit number P1097 to the revised military lexicon. The Chamber has since been informed by the Registry that the Rule 65 ter number it was instructed to assign an exhibit number to was not the military lexicon but an already existing exhibit, namely, P1020, admitted pursuant to the decision on Prosecution's 7th motion to admit evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, a decision which was delivered on the 6th of February, 2013. For purposes of correcting the record, the Chamber clarifies that the revised military lexicon bears Rule 65 ter number 28678 and not as it was read out on the record, or at least as it appears on the transcript, on the 1st of March, Rule 65 ter 28687. It seems that the last two digits have been mixed up. Noting that P1097 has, in the meantime, been used for another Rule 65 ter number, the Chamber kindly instructs the Registry to assign a new exhibit number to Rule 65 ter 28678, which is the military lexicon. I move to the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar says that she's ready to assign a new exhibit number to Rule 65 ter 28678. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28678 receives number P1116, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1116, the military lexicon, is admitted into evidence. I move on to my next item. On the 1st of March of this year, the Chamber, upon a Prosecution request, invited the Registry to amend the description on e-court in relation to admitted Exhibit P143. The parties have previously been informed of the procedure in this regard but the Chamber takes this opportunity to remind everyone thereof. The parties give descriptions to Rule 65 ter documents. Once a document is admitted, the Registry will give a neutral description of the document solely based on the content of the document. For technical reasons, the party descriptions may still be visible for exhibits on e-court, but they do not form part of the exhibit and will not appear once the public exhibits are put on the public judicial database. The Chamber, in any event, does not rely on the descriptions but on the content of the documents. Now, with regard to P143, the Prosecution is seeking a change in the description on e-court and presumably in the surrogate sheet. Accordingly, the Prosecution should upload an amended surrogate sheet under a new doc ID number and inform the Registry thereof. This newly uploaded document should then also contain the matching meta data. Until this is done, P143 is MFI'd. I move on to my next item. The document D199 was MFI'd due to an incomplete English translation. On the 28th of February of this year, the Defence notified that they had received the CLSS translation of D199 and sought permission, if the Prosecution agreed, to replace the English translation currently in e-court with the doc ID 1D02-3637. The Prosecution notified, on the 1st of March, per e-mail, that it agreed to this. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the translation and admits D199 into evidence. I move on to the next item. On the 6th of March, the Chamber was informed by the Prosecution that the B/C/S translation of Exhibit P866, which was admitted through Witness RM157, was uploaded in e-court as doc ID Y003-4753-B/C/S T, in capitals. The Registry is instructed to attach the B/C/S translation to the English original. Next item. On the 1st of March, 2013, the Defence informed the Chamber that a full B/C/S version of MFI D118, including the cover page, as requested by the Chamber, has been uploaded into e-court as doc ID number 1D02-3677 and requests leave to replace the current version in e-court with this complete translation. Is there any objection from the Prosecution's part?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber then requests the Registry to replace doc ID number 1D01-2871 with the complete B/C/S version uploaded as doc 1D02-3677 and hereby admits Exhibit D118 into evidence. Next item deals with D44 MFI'd. Per e-mail of the 25th of January, 2013, the Chamber inquired with the Defence whether it still intends to tender D44; and, if so, when the Chamber can expect the transcripts of the video in question, as well as the position of the Prosecution in this regard. The Chamber raised the matter in court on the 1st of March, 2013, but the Defence was not able to reply at that moment. We have, as yet, not received any response to our questions, and the Chamber wonders whether the parties are in a position to provide the Chamber with an update in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will definitely have to check with our Case Manager --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- on the status of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we hear from you -- well, let's say, if possible, today at least, if not, then by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll do the same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I move on to my next item. On the 28th of February, 2013 - and the issue is about P512 MFI'd - the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to re-visit P512, in light of its decision on the associated exhibits of Witness Thomas and to inform the Chamber once it has done so. On the 14th of March, 2013, the Prosecution informed the Chamber, through an informal communication, that a revised version of P512 has been uploaded in e-court under 65 ter number 19703b. This is herewith put on the record, and the Chamber instructs the Registry to replace the current version in e-court with the revised version and admits this version into evidence. I move on to the next item relating to Exhibit P706. On the 19th of February, the Prosecution informed per e-mail that it had located another English translation of the B/C/S original admitted as P706 which, it submits, more accurately reflects the B/C/S original and seeks permission, subject to agreement from the Defence, to replace the current English translation with this newly identified translation. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no objections. Then the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the document bearing ERN 0303-3680-0303-3688 with the new English translation bearing ERN 0301-2528-0301-2536. The next item deals with the Defence request for additional time to respond to the 20th and the 21st Rule 92 bis motion. The Chamber puts on the record its decision to grant the Defence's request filed on the 21st of March of this year for an additional 60 days to respond to the Prosecution's 20th and 21st Rule 92 bis motions, communicated informally to the parties on that same day. I hereby note that the deadline, thus, becomes the 27th of May, 2013. The next item deals with the anticipated date of filing of Defence Rule 94 bis (B) notice with respect to six forensic expert witnesses. On 28th of March, 2013, the Chamber notified the Defence that the Defence was expected to filed its Rule 94 bis (B) notice with respect to the six proposed forensic expert witnesses noticed in the Prosecution's 7th of November, 2012, filing by the 22nd of April, 2013. Is there anything the parties would like to add in relation of this data filing of the 94 bis (B) notice? If not, I move on -- which I move on to an item dealing with Exhibit P1016. The document bearing Rule 65 ter number 28685 was admitted into evidence by the Chamber's decision on Prosecution's 7th motion to admit evidence, pursuant to Rule 92 bis, a decision of the 6th of February, 2013, and on the 27th of February it was assigned exhibit number P1016. This document was unredacted, while, by the Chamber's decision, it was admitted in redacted form. By e-mail dated the 6th of March, 2013, the Prosecution informed the Chamber that it had uploaded the document in redacted form under Rule 65 ter number 28685a. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to remove the unredacted version and replace it with the redacted version. I move on to the next item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. In -- in thinking about your previous subject of the -- the experts, that the Defence is supposed to tell us their response, and that -- that's a particularly important response for us to hear as you can imagine. There's people coming from all over the world. We have provided the Defence some of the translations that they requested 3/4/2013. However, there's an ongoing discussion that we're having with them. They have suggested they would like translations of -- of autopsy reports and we have never translated the thousands of autopsy reports we have for the pathologist for Srebrenica, and we have -- have entered into informal discussions with them about that. But that's something that we do need to get decided between ourselves very soon because it will hold up everything that we are doing. And so I hope to speak to Mr. Lukic about that, but I did want to alert you that that is a potential issue. It's a very large amount of translations that we have never done and we hope to work that out with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are they new or are they used in other cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They're old. They've been around since the Krstic case, most of them, that we're talking that are related to our OTP pathologist that did the autopsies for the first few years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is it that you want to have translations of some of them which are of particular concern to you, or do you say just all of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's better to talk with Mr. McCloskey during the break, and I think my co-counsel Mr. Stojanovic is much better expert on that issue, since they dealt with all of them previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll wait for the result of such a conversation. I'm not going to advise you on whether to have a cup of coffee or a cup of tea with it, but that's where we are. Then I move on to my next item, which deals with the confidential status of exhibits which were tendered through Witness RM513. Pursuant to an instruction by the Chamber on the 1st of March, 2013 - I'm referring to transcript page 9494 - the Prosecution has made submissions by e-mail with regard to the confidential status of several documents tendered through Witness RM513. The Prosecution's position is that any exhibits which bear the witness's name, directly relate to the witness's employment or otherwise create a risk of identifying the witness should be under seal. This includes the following: Exhibits P1053; P1054; P1057 up to and including P1060; P1091 up to and including P1096; as well as Exhibits D255; D257; D259; and D260, which were the only four documents which were eventually tendered by the Defence. The others which were mentioned in the Prosecution's e-mail have been vacated. The Prosecution further submits that P1063, which had tentatively been placed under seal, should be made public. Finally, with regard to P1096, MFI, the Prosecution submits that this document will be tendered as a public exhibit through a different witness. My question to the Defence is whether there are any objections with regard to the confidential status of these documents as I read them out a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If the Prosecution thinks that it should be closed because of the safety of the witness, we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Then the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to update the status of these exhibits accordingly and to vacate Exhibit number P1096. I have dealt with all of the technical issues. I refrain at this moment, Mr. Lukic, from reading any oral decisions which are not known yet to the Defence. Are there any other matters any of the parties would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one technical procedural matter that might be appropriate to deal with at this point in time. Your Honours, the Defence, on the 2nd of April, 2013, filed a response to the Prosecution motion for admission of utterances of Mr. Mladic. The Prosecution is in the process of assessing whether it will file a reply. I raise this for -- simply for the following procedural reason. In paragraph 25 of the Defence response, the Defence writes: "The Defence renews its motion seeking a reduction in the number of sitting days based on the deteriorated health of the accused." There is no specific relief in this regard sought in the relief section of that response. The Prosecution seeks guidance from the Chamber whether paragraph 25 in the response will be deemed a formal motion to which the Prosecution should respond. It would be the Prosecution's preference that if the Defence do intend to file another motion with respect to the -- the sitting schedule, that it be done in a separate filing so that the Prosecution can respond to that issue fully. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our intention is to file separate motion, Your Honour, in accordance with the -- the letter we received on the 2nd of April, and as attachment we received the 20th of March, 2013, letter from reporting medical officer from the UNDU who also proposed to have four-day sitting during the week. So, yes, we will file separate motion, or, if you want me, I can have an oral motion right now. Whatever is your preference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the matter is not simple. I would suggest that you file a separate motion and that you agree that the Chamber will not -- in its decision on the motion for admission for utterances of Mr. Mladic will not deal with the request as contained in the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll file the separate motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that's clear. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, is there any update as far as the medical reporting of the accused is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honours. I just checked with the Detention Unit. They're waiting for a report to be submitted by the nurse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, by the way, I should have mentioned, that you had requested to be allowed to have your mobile phone in court so that you could receive any text messages updating you on the situation. And, of course, the Chamber has no objections to that. Now the question is, did you read anything on your little screen or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet. Then I suggest that we adjourn or take a break, depending on what messages we will receive. I think it would be wise anyhow to perhaps briefly come back to court once we have received any medical report. And, therefore, the parties are instructed to remain stand by. We adjourn either for later today or until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there -- let me see ... Mr. Lukic, can there anything you learned, meanwhile, which could assist the Chamber in dealing with the present situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we cannot contact directly our client at the UNDU, I called my legal consultant, Ivetic, to try to contact the UNDU and try to reach Mr. Mladic to give consent for this medical documentation be provided for the Chamber and the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we do not know yet whether he has given it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He hasn't, for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He has not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because he has not been contacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, anything else you have learned or is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing more than you know from the Registrar, because I'm talking to Madam Registrar as well and I know what you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me, first, put on the record what we have received until now. We have received a form titled: "Absence from court due to illness," which consists of a declaration, and it's split up in three parts. The first: "I am unable to attend court proceedings on this date due to illness." That box is ticked which we understand to be that Mr. Mladic says that he is unable to attend court proceedings due to illness. The second box: "I have discussed the matter with counsel." That box is -- it's a bit unclear. There is something ticked, but I'll re-visit this issue later. Then the third item on this form is not ticked, and that's the one where a person involved would state that he knows his rights and that he waives. So, therefore, the Chamber understands that there is no waiver at this moment. There is a handwritten addition in Cyrillic, which we have not yet received in a formal translation. This absence from court due to illness form apparently is signed by Mr. Mladic. We have a report from the principal officer, and I read the relevant portions. "I confirm receipt of this form from the detainee named over at 0855." The -- it refers to the part of the form I just did put on the record signed by Mr. Mladic. In the box "Other comments," it reads: "He did sign but he didn't get in contact yet with his counsel. He is trying it from 9.00." The Chamber understands this that Mr. Mladic has had no opportunity to consult with counsel but that he's seeking to establish contact. Then we have -- the second half of this page of the report is the UNDU medical service where it says questions 1, 2, 4, and 5 must be answered, 3, not necessarily. Box under, number 1, is ticked which reads: "I confirm that I've examined the detainee named on the preceding page." Boxes 2A and 2B, and I read it, they're not ticked. Not the first one, 2A; not the second one, 2B. "I confirm that he has observable symptoms which indicate that he may feel too unwell to attend court." This therefore was not established. 2B: "I confirm that he has no observable symptoms with which I can judge whether or not he is too unwell to attend court." Again, not ticked. On question 4, 4A, which is -- the box is ticked: "Including today, I assess that he will require a one-day absence before he should be fit to attend court once more." Then the several options under 5. 5C is ticked: "The medical officer will see the detainee today." What is not ticked is 5B, the medical officer has seen the detainee. Other comments, 6: "The specialist recommended him not to go to court for today." This is signed by J. Nordan, and it's added VPKMO, which the Chamber interprets as the nurse. The Chamber was not aware of any specialist involvement and wondered what specialist had recommended Mr. Mladic not to go to court for today. We sought information through the Registry, and the following appeared to us. Mr. Mladic has been in Bronovo hospital early this morning. That's what we learned. We have not received any indication on whether there was any urgency matter or not, and, therefore, the Chamber certainly considers it a reasonable possibility, because, otherwise, we would have informed about any urgent matter, that it was a routine or a pre-scheduled visit to the Bronovo hospital for whatever reasons. The Chamber inquired with the UNDU to at least know what kind of specialist it was that Mr. Mladic has visited this morning, and this information was not provided to us, so we have got no idea what specialist he consulted this morning, neither do we have any idea -- well, what -- what diagnosis there was, which allowed already to say that it would last only for one day. Which means that, at this moment, based on a recommendation - not even being clear who gave this information to the nurse - without any observable symptoms having been considered by the nurse who wrote this, and purely on the basis of what, most likely, is a routine visit to the Bronovo to a specialist unknown to the Chamber but apparently pre-scheduled, that we are now informed that we should, for medical reasons, not continue. That's at least the gist of what we see. Under those circumstances, the Chamber considers, as matters stand now, that there's no medical reason not to proceed. Therefore, the Chamber will give an opportunity to the parties to make further observations on this initial analysis of the present situation and we'll then decide whether or not we will proceed. I give an opportunity, Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that there are two things that I would have -- the Prosecution would have concern with, with respect to the Chamber's analysis. One is with respect to the failure to check 2A, 2B. The Chamber seems to be drawing the -- or concluding from the failure for the person who filled out this form to check either box that there were no observable symptoms, and that does -- from my understanding it does not seem that it excludes the possibility that the person made an inadvertent error when they failed to check that, so I wonder whether the Chamber would want to make an inquiry from this person. I remind the Chamber that there is the videolink, so in a few minutes this nurse could be on the video screen and available to answer questions by the Chamber to -- to confirm what exactly this person observed this morning. And then the second thing, Your Honour, with respect to Bronovo hospital, I think that in fairness would require some more detailed information about whether Mr. Mladic had any control over being sent to Bronovo this morning. Even if it was a regularly scheduled appointment, it would seem that if he had no voluntary way of not going, was simply sent there, it seems that the fault would lie not with Mr. Mladic for his absence but with the Registry for not informing the Chamber that it had made arrangements to have him see a doctor or specialist in Bronovo today. Those would be the two concerns that the Prosecution would have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How we see this is -- regarding this 2A and 2B, it might even that be the nurse at this moment didn't see Mr. Mladic but she only was actually leaning on the recommendation of the specialist. And from the practice, we know that it cannot be scheduled visit at this early hours of the morning. Scheduled visits usually take place after 11.00, as we know. So having in mind this time, we think it was something urgent, and we -- we probably need another break to inquire about this waiver. I don't think that Mr. Mladic will not give it. The only thing is to contact him through the regular channels of the UNDU, and sometimes it does take time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me briefly -- if you're finished --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me briefly address the matters raised. First, not ticking the boxes 2A and 2B, the suggestion that it might have been inadvertently done, for the Chamber, seems not to be the most likely interpretation. First of all, the report was written by a nurse; but, still, a nurse can observe anything. But from the information the Chamber received, we concluded that it was exclusively on the basis of a recommendation, and we do not know whether it was a direct recommendation to the nurse by the Bronovo hospital or by the specialist, or whether it was conveyed to the nurse by Mr. Mladic. Since not knowing this, of course, what we would like to know is what kind of a visit it was. Now, the UNDU medical services has refused to give us information as to whether it's an ear, nose and throat specialist or whatever. I can imagine that if it would have been an urgent -- sending Mr. Mladic to the cardiologist in Bronovo hospital that the situation might have been different. But if there would have been an urgent matter causing the UNDU medical services to send Mr. Mladic to Bronovo hospital, we, the Chamber, should have been informed about. It is unimaginable for this Chamber that such an urgency would not immediately be reported to us, and the information we received through the Registry does not hint in any way to such an urgent matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interrupt, I'm sorry, I just got the information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- which is very fresh. Maybe it can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says that the report -- actually, that Mr. Mladic cannot sign anything before 1.00 p.m., since the medical doctor cannot be there before 1.00, compose the report, and after he composes the report, Mr. Mladic can sign it. Only afterwards. So we cannot expect anything before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That is a practical piece of information. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you inform us about the medical doctor, which medical doctor that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Falke. Dr. Falke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Falke. Yes, that is the UNDU -- okay. Now, I continue where I stopped. That -- that is, that apparently on the basis of a recommendation - and apparently exclusively on that - not knowing how it was conveyed, that we are supposed not to continue for medical reasons. Mr. Lukic, the first and, of course, important thing also, would be to hear from Mr. Mladic whether he would agree for us to know what kind of specialist he saw. Mr. Lukic, you've also seen then, most likely, a handwritten note. Can you -- it's apparently read in Cyrillic. Could you read to us what you see there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says: "Or RM" in Cyrillic, but I think it should be GRM, General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that it could be O-r-i, Orie, a message to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would read it as GRM. And it said: "Sleeping out." I think that he wanted to send a message, short message, that he is going to sleep because he doesn't feel well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then, of course -- let me -- I receive an e-mail at this moment. Mr. Lukic, just allow me a second to read it. I -- I will put on the record the information as we receive it now, which is the -- a message from the officer in charge of the United Nations Detention Unit, and he, first of all, informs us that the medical officer in line with the normal attendance schedule will be present in the UNDU this afternoon, which seems to confirm, Mr. Lukic, what you said. He apparently also informed the officer in charge of the UN Detention Unit that Mr. Mladic attended a pre-scheduled consultation with a specialist at an external hospital early this morning. The consultation included a minor invasive procedure, and afterwards, the specialist recommended that Mr. Mladic rest for the remainder of day. I understand from the medical officer that this is a possibility for this type of procedure, but it is also common that patients are able to continue as normal. And the medical officer has offered to put this information in writing this afternoon. We'll consider all of this, and I'll now continue with the preliminary observations in relation to the observations made by the parties. We have dealt with the inadvertent -- the possibility of an inadvertent not ticking out. From what I have now just read, it may well be that the nurse has not either confirmed that she did see observable symptoms, but also that she was also not confident to confirm that he has no observable symptoms which would allow the nurse to draw any further conclusions. The second one was whether it was regular or scheduled. Mr. Lukic, I think you'll be very happy that if you need an appointment at any hospital in The Hague, that they will receive you early in the morning so that you can attend court in time. I must the same as is my experience. Going to hospital early in the morning allows you to be in time in court. I think this is sufficiently cleared up now by the message I just read, that it was a pre-scheduled visit. The Chamber, by the way, would have been -- would have welcomed to be informed about this kind of appointment, which clearly are at risk to have an impact on the court proceedings. Yes, we have dealt with the early hours. What then remains is that the specialist apparently recommended - I don't know how this was conveyed; we still do not know - that Mr. Mladic take rest for the rest of the day. We still do not know what kind of diagnosis or what exactly it was. The minor invasive issue, we do not know what it is. I suggest that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to briefly discuss among themselves the information it has reached the Chamber and then decide on whether or not to proceed today or to wait until tomorrow. Meanwhile, Mr. Lukic, if you would have -- if Mr. Ivetic would have any opportunity to check with Mr. Mladic about giving us the information, that might be relevant for us, and if there would be any possibility, either through videolink or otherwise, to be in touch with Mr. -- Dr. Falke to further assess the necessity of not sitting today, the Registry is invited to create communication between the Chamber and Dr. Falke or the specialist in the hospital, the external hospital. We don't know yet how much time we would need for it. We'll take a break, and the parties are invited to remain stand by. --- Break taken at 11.37 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we continue, is there any new information you can provide us with?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any new information from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber has carefully considered and analysed the situation at present and has decided that we'll not proceed today, that we'll adjourn for the day, and that we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 9th of April, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of April, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.04 p.m.,
